list.listitem: Heart failure is a syndrome resulting from a variety of cardiac pathologies, but typified by elevated cardiac filling pressures and/or a reduction in cardiac output. A
The absence of clinical manifestations and a normal chest X-ray do not exclude the diagnosis, which it is important to have high clinical intuition. C

Treatments effective in decreasing symptoms, reducing hospitalizaitons, and/or prolonging life include: ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, β-blockers, SGLT-2 inhibitors,and aldosterone antagonists.A
Diuretics can be helpful to alleviate symptoms of congestion but does not reduce mortality. A
Patients should be educated about early symptoms, common triggers, and the importance of monitoring their weight in order to decrease mortality and frequent hospitlizations. C

background.definition: Heart failure is a syndrome resulting from the heart's inability to maintain adequate cardiac output to the tissues and to maintain normal cardiac filling pressures. Symptoms include edema, shortness of breath, and effort intolerance. One cause of heart failure is myocardial muscle dysfunction characterized by left ventricular dilation or hypertrophy. Systolic heart failure is characterized by a reduced ejection fraction (<40%).

list.listitem: 550,000 patients a year diagnosed in United States.
A total of 2% of the population older than 45 years has left ventricular dysfunction defined by an ejection fraction <40%.
Approximately 5 million patients in the United States.
The proportion of deaths due to heart failure has increased sharply as the incidence and prevalence of the disease has increased.
Ischemic heart disease
Hypertension
Diabetes mellitus
Dilated cardiomyopathy (may have a genetic cause vs. amylodosis
Valvular dysfunction
Thryoid DysfunctionAnemia
Chemotherapeutic agents (trastuzumab, anthracyclines)
Poor contractility and decreased left ventricular compliance due to diminished systolic function, results in decreased cardiac output and increased cardiac filling pressures.
Reduced cardiac output stimulates activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and other neurohormonal pathways. Over time this causes ventricular hypertrophy and progressive dysfunction.

Patients with heart failure may present with dyspnea, peripheral edema, or fatigue. A substantial proportion of patients will not present with symptoms, but will experience dyspnea with exertion, if tested. C
The absence of classical signs of heart failure does not rule out the diagnosis. Diagnosis is clinical. C
A normal chest X-ray does not exclude the diagnosis. C
The presence of an S3 gallop on exam in patients with respiratory symptoms strongly supports the diagnosis.

Differential.Differential_Name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and Internstial Lung Disease
Differential.Differential_Features: The BNP level is likely to be more elevated in patients with heart failure than in those with COPD
Deconditioning may lead to dyspnea on exertion, but other symptoms of heart failure—except dependent edema—will not be present
Chest pain or pressure rather than dyspnea limits exertion
BNP level usually normal, other signs of heart failure absent
Acute onset, unilateral leg swelling, leg pain more common in VTE

list.listitem: The European Society of Cardiology definition of heart failure, including both systolic and diastolic heart failure (the first 2 should be fulfilled in all cases) includes: (1) Symptoms of heart failure (at rest or during exercise); (2) Objective evidence (preferably by echocardiography) of cardiac dysfunction (systolic and/or diastolic); and (3) in cases where the diagnosis is in doubt, response to treatment directed toward heart failure.

Patients with heart failure may present with exertional dyspnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopena, peripheral edema, or fatigue. A substantial proportion of patients will not present with symptoms, but will experience dyspnea with exertion, if tested.
The clinical examination is frequently unreliable for diagnosing heart failure, particularly in the elderly.
Elements of the history that best rule in heart failure are history of heart failure or history of myocardial infarction.

Many of the classical signs of heart failure, such as elevated jugular venous pressure, third heart sound, abdominojugular reflux, and rales are specific but lack sensitivity; that is, if present, they help to establish the diagnosis, but their absence does not rule out the diagnosis.

Clinical judgment that the patient does not have heart failure, combined with a normal BNP level (<100 pg/mL) significantly decreases the likelihood of heart failure. Point of care testing of BNP levels may help to exclude the diagnosis of heart failure in some settings.
Common causes of heart failure exacerbations include nonadherence to medications, recrational drug use such as coccaine, salt indiscretion, respiratory tract infections, arrhythmias, and medications.
The clinical finding of bendopnea (shortness of breath after bending over while seated) is marker of worsening symptoms in heart failure.
Point of care ultrasound can be effective in estimating jugular venous pressure, but traditional diagnosis is as accurate (when the JVP is visualized).
Recommended initial laboratory investigations include CBC, electrolytes, blood lipids, thyroid function, and UDS to look for reversible causes of heart failure.

ECG and CXR are also part of the initial evaluation. Few patients with heart failure have a completely normal ECG, but the changes are nonspecific. A normal chest X-ray does not exclude the diagnosis of heart failure, but can help identify alternate causes of dyspnea.
The BNP test has high sensitivity; that is, a normal value of BNP helps to exclude the diagnosis of heart failure. It is also useful in patients with a previous diagnosis of heart failure.

BNP may help distinguish heart failure from lung disease in the emergency department (ED), as the BNP level will generally be higher in patients with heart failure. However, there is a substantial overlap in values.

In an RCT in a Swiss ED, the use of BNP reduced admissions to hospitals and, therefore, reduced costs. A Canadian study of patients presenting to the ED with dyspnea supported the Swiss study results finding that N-terminal BNP (NT-BNP) reduced the cost of care, the length of the ED visit, and the likelihood of rehospitalization. However, two other studies did not find this benefit.

In a meta-analysis of six studies of patients with chronic heart failure (only one was double-blinded) testing BNP or NT-BNP guided care (including use of specific care guidelines in five of the trials), monitoring BNP decreased mortality as a result of more aggressive treatment (HR = 0.69; 95% CI, 0.55-0.86). The benefit was more pronounced in patients younger than 75 years. A recent RCT confirmed these findings and reported that the combination of NT-BNP monitoring and dosage titration significantly decreased mortality at 1 year compared with usual care (9.1% vs 18.9%; NNT = 10.2) and at 3 years for patients younger than 75 years (15.5% vs 30.9% and 31.3%).
A study comparing inpatient therapy guided by BNP in elderly patients with heart failure with care not guided by BNP found no major differences in clinical outcomes.
Screening with BNP in a high risk population was associated with a decreased risk of emergent hospitalization for heart failure.

A clinical decision rule to identify patients with heart failure among those presenting with dyspnea in the ED has been developed and validated. The clinical decision rule uses the BNP and seven clinical variables.

Another prognostic rule, developed in more than 33,000 inpatients and validated in a second group of 32,000, uses clinical and laboratory variables to estimate the prognosis of patients with acutely decompensated heart failure. A second well-validated rule by Lee and colleagues can determine prognosis for any patient hospitalized with heart failure.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to the patient with suspected heart failure.

Treatments effective in decreasing symptoms, reducing hospitalizaitons, and/or prolonging life include: ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (with or without neprilysin inhibitors), β-blockers, SGLT-2 inhibitors,and aldosterone antagonists.A
Diuretics can be helpful to alleviate symptoms of congestion. A
Sprinolactone and Eplerenone, for patients with systolic dysfunction after myocardial infarction. A
Small trials have shown that diuretics improve symptoms and may reduce mortality. A
Digoxin may improve symptoms but also may increase mortality, especially in women. However, a Cochrane review found no mortality difference. A
Exercise training improves symptoms and may reduce long term all-cause mortality.A

listitem.strong: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers

list.listitem: A systematic review of trials of ACE inhibitors versus placebo showed that over the longer term (approximately 1 year), mortality was reduced from 27% to 23% (NNT = 25).
Higher doses of ACE inhibitors have been shown to reduce hospitalizations, although this result needs to be balanced against the increased rate of side effects, particularly dizziness.

While some studies have shown angiotensin II receptor blockers have similar effectiveness as ACE inhibitors and should be used for patients who cannot tolerate ACE inhibitors. Other reviews have not shown morbidity or mortality benefit in angiotensin II receptor blockers in either systolic dysfunction or in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.
Neprilysin inhibition (with sacubitril) in addition to angiotensin receptor blockade is associated with reduced death and heart failure admissions when compared to ACE inhibition alone.

18 trials comparing β-blockers versus placebo in patients taking standard medications for heart failure (mostly ACE inhibitors) showed a significant survival benefit at adequate doses (OR = 0.69; 95% CI, 0.54-0.88). Approximately 10% of patients cannot be titrated to the full dose because of bradycardia. Commence β-blockers once condition is stable. A recent systematic review failed to identify the superiority of one betal blocker over another for improving survival with heart failure on comparing carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, and bisoprolol.

Diuretics have only been evaluated against placebo in 7 small trials, but these trials showed reduced mortality and hospital admissions. In 7 trials comparing diuretics with other agents for heart failure (eg, ACE inhibitors), diuretics were shown to improve exercise tolerance.

Bolus diuretics (intravenous furosemide dosed equal to [low dose strategy] or 2.5 times [high dose strategy] the home daily oral dose) was as effective as a continuous infusion of diuretics for the treatment of acute decompensated heart failure with regard to improvement in symptoms. Higher doses of bolus diuretics are associated with improved breathlessness, increased diuresis and increased weight reduction at the expense of increasing the risk of azotemia.
In a single pragmatic trial, torsemide has not been shown to have mortality benefit over furosemide for outpatients with HFpEF.
In patients with acute decompensated heart failure (and eGFR>20), addition of acetazolamide to loop diuretics was effective in relieving congestion.

Spironolactone improves outcomes in patients who are symptomatic while using an ACE inhibitor and a loop diuretic, reducing mortality from 46% to 35% over 2 years (NNT = 9) and reducing hospitalizations (NNT = 11). Spironolactone is contraindicated if the patient has renal failure or a potassium level of greater than 5.0 mEq/L (5.0 mmol/L).

Eplerenone (an aldosterone antagonist) reduced mortality in patients who had a left ventricular ejection fraction of less than 40% following myocardial infarction. It does not appear to be more effective than older aldosterone antagonists such as spironolactone.
Aldosterone antagonsists are associated with reduced mortality in heart failure in patients <75 years old; the benefit in older patients is less clear.
Several meta-analyses have demonstrated reduction in all cause and cardiovascular mortality in heart failure patients treated with SGLT-2 inhibitors.

Dapagliflozin (an SGLT-2 inhibitor used for glycemic control in type 2 diabetes) was shown to reduce health care utilization (NNT 27 over 18 months) and all-cause mortality (NNT = 44 over 18 months) compared to placebo in NYHA class II heart failure, irrespective of co-existing diabetes.

A randomized trial assigned 3730 patients with Class II-IV HF to empagliflozin 10 mg once daily or placebo. Patients who took the drug were less likely to be hospitalized for heart failure (HF), but there was no difference in the likelihood of cardiovascular death. Although benefit was seen in patients with and without diabetes, the benefit appears limited to patients with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of less than 30% and is less impressive in white patients and patients who are obese.

A study randomized 6522 patients with acute MI and high risk for HF to empagliflozin or placebo. For the outcomes of first hospitalization for HF or all-cause death after 18 months, there was no significant difference between the 2 groups (8.2% in the empagliflozin group vs 9.1% in the placebo group; P = .21). When looking at individual components of the composite endpoint, patients in the empagliflozin group had a slight reduction in HF hospitalizations (3.6% vs.4.7%; hazard ratio 0.77; 95% CI 0.60 - 0.98). The percentage of serious adverse events leading to drug discontinuation was the same in the 2 groups (3.8%).

The DIG trial suggests that only men with heart failure benefit from digoxin and that the optimal digoxin range is 0.5 ng/mL to 0.8 ng/mL. In the same trial, digoxin increased mortality, especially in women. A Cochrane review of 13 RCTs of digoxin in patients with HF in sinus rhythm found no mortality difference although digitalis therapy was associated with a lower rate of hospitalization and of clinical deterioration.

There is preliminary evidence from a large RCT of a reduction in mortality and cardiovascular events with warfarin in patients with heart failure. Other evidence would suggest that there is no benefit for routine use of warfarin in heart failure where subjects are in sinus rhythm.
There is no evidence from long-term trials that use of aspirin prevents thromboembolism in patients with heart failure in sinus rhythm.

Isosorbide dinitrate plus hydralazine improved survival and quality of life and reduced hospital admission rates in patients with left ventricular systolic dysfunction who identified themselves as black or of African descent.

Nesiritide is a natriuretic peptide that reduces afterload. In a study of 101 patients with moderate to severe HF, adding nesiritide to standard therapy in the ED did not affect 30 day readmission rates or hospitalizations. A randomized controlled trial found no significant improvement in breathlessness, mortality, or rehospitalization for heart failure in subjects treated with nesiritide versus placebo for acute decompensated heart failure. Nesiritide was associated with increased hypotension relative to placebo.
Treatment of patients with heart failure with normal lipids with rosuvastatin does not improve clinical outcomes.
The use of phosphodiesterase inhibitors in symptomatic patients with heart failure is associated with a significant (17%) increased mortality rate (RR = 1.17; 95% CI, 1.06-1.30).
Vericiguat, a guanylate cyclase stimulator, significantly reduced HF hospitalizations with a NNT of 45 at 10.8 months of follow-up. However, there was no effect on mortality.

Treating iron deficiency, defined as ferritin <100 or ferritin 100-300 with transferrin saturation < 20%, with IV iron reduces mortality and improves quality of life in patients with systolic heart failure.

Five trials showed that implantable defibrillators reduce mortality in patients with nonischemic cardiomyopathy, but do not decrease mortality when implanted within the first 40 days following myocardial infarction in ischemic cardiomyopathy. One meta-analysis of five trials failed to demonstrate a statistical all-cause mortality benefit among women with heart failure who receive implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (HR = 1.01; 95% CI, 0.76-1.33).
Cardiac resynchronization (such as a combined pacemaker/defibrillator) reduces mortality and hospitalization in patients with heart failure and interventricular conduction delay.

Meta-analysis of 6 RCTs involving 775 showed that atrial fibrillation ablation, when compared to drug therapy in patients with systolic heart failure, reduced all-casue mortality (NNT = 12), HF hospitalizations (NNT = 9), improved left ventricular ejection fraction (NNT = 13), 6-minute walk test distance, peak oxygen consumption and quality of life. The number of serious adverse were not significantly different between the ablation and medical therapy groups.

A recent study of 23 patients has shown His bundle pacing (HSP) is more effective at delivering ventricular resynchronization than biventricular pacing. Additionally, it reduces QRS duration, left ventricular activation time, and left ventricular dyssynchrony index while improving acute hemodynamic response.

Surgical revascularization with coronary bypass surgery has been shown to reduce cardiovascular death and a composite of hospitalization and death from any cause in subjects with ischemic cardiomyopathy and ejection fraction less than 35%. Overall mortality is not affected. Preoperative measurement of myocardial viability does not predict improved cardiovascular survival or overall survival after surgery.

Percutaneous coronary intervention for patients with extensive coronary artery disease and an ischemic cardiomyopathy (EF<35%) provided no clear benefit relative to medical therapy in one clinical trial.
A Cochrane review of 14 RCTs found significant benefit in symptom control and exercise tolerance from hawthorn extract as an adjunctive treatment for chronic heart failure.
Tai Chi may be of benefit in patients with cardiovascular disease, including heart failure, by decreasing blood pressure and improving exercise capacity.
In limited studies, use of Shengmai (a traditional Chinese herbal preparation) may improve symptoms of heart failure.

Exercise training: 19 trials (including one large trial) with 6 month follow-up or longer demonstrated significant improvement in health-related quality of life with exercise training and appears to reduce heart failure-related hospital admissions. Althoughxercise did not affect all-cause mortality in the short term (<12 months), but may reduce it in the long term (>12 months; 6 trials with 2845 participants).
Although depression is common in patients with heart failure, evidence showing benefit for psychological interventions are limited.
Support smoking cessation.

Education, follow-up by a specialist nurse, and telephone follow-up all reduce readmissions in patients recently discharged from the hospital. Adherence to professional society performance measures has not been shown to decrease 30-day readmission rates or mortality. Pharmacist-directed interventions have not been shown to be effective at reducing hospitalizations.

In another study, discharge instructions for a sodium-restricted diet was associated with a reduced risk of 30-day mortality and readmission. A recent systematic review, however, found no morbidity or mortality benefit in adherence to a sodium-restricted diet. There are limited high quality trials to assess this question.

In a study of 1029 patients with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema, CPAP, and NIPPV do not reduce mortality or intubation more than standard oxygen therapy, but do provide a benefit in terms of dyspnea. Overall, NIPPV is safe and effective in the treatment of cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
Readmission is not uncommon after heart failure hospitalization. Moderate evidence supports home nursing visits and multidisciplinary clinic to reduce readmissions.
Iron infusions may improve clinical outcomes in patients with heart failure who are iron deficient.
Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation improves survival in patients admitted to the hospital with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
Continuous infusion of loop diuretics appears to improve survival and to reduce the risk of tinnitus and hearing loss.
The 5-year mortality rate is 25% to 75%. B
Death may be due to sudden cardiac death (mostly ventricular arrhythmias) or to a slow progression of disease. B
The 5-year mortality rate varies widely (25%-75%), depending on the etiology of the patient's cardiomyopathy.
Death may be due to sudden cardiac death (mostly ventricular arrhythmias) or to a slow progression of disease.
Weight loss-cariac cachexia is a poor prognostic sign. Other signs of poor prognosis are frequent hospitalizations, the inability to complete any activity without dyspnea, or symptoms at rest.
An elevated cardiac troponin I or T level is associated with longer hospital stay and worse in-hospital mortality.
BNP for improvement has now been recommmended for AHA guidelinesAssess exercise capacity, change in weight, patient adherence to medication, and assessment of symptoms.
Assess presence of ischemic heart disease, diabetic control, hypertension, and the presence or any triggering factors.
Monitor electrolytes and renal function if there's been a recent change in management, otherwise assess every 6 months.
Avoid TCAs, NSAIDs, and thiazolidinediones (e.g., rosiglitazone).
Naturetic peptide testing is not superior to usual care in long term management.
Educate patients about potential triggers to avoid rehospitlizatio
Educate patients, proper salt restriction (<2g daily), and fluid restrition.
Educate patients, proper salt restriction (<2 g daily), and fluid restriction
Patients should weigh themselves and report any gain of more than 1 to 2 kg over a few days.
Advise patients to have regular influenza and pneumococcal vaccinations.
Provide patients with support for smoking and/or recreational use disorder.
Provide patients with support for cessation of excessive alcohol intake.
The diagnosis of heart failure is more difficult in the elderly.

Also see diastolic heart failure. Diastolic heart failure (i.e., heart failure with preserved ejection fraction or HFpEF) patients are generally older, more likely to be female, and more likely to have a history of hypertension.

algorithm.title: Algorithm for the Management of Heart Failure.

cell.label: Suspected heart failure: Patient older than 60 years who presents with dyspnea, fatigue, or edema. Most will have a history of ischemic heart disease or hypertension or diabetes
ECG, BNP, and CXR (primarily to exclude other causes of dyspnea).
Evaluate for other causes of symptoms.
Urine and electrolytes, creatinine, LFT, TFT, glucose, lipids, echocardiogram.
Assess for triggers, reversible causes, and underlying cardiovascular disease.
Use ACE inhibitor (or ARB) and β-blocker plus diuretic for symptoms.
If still symptomatic, consider spironolactone (if no renal failure or hyperkalaemia), digoxin (if in sinus rhythm), hydralazine, or isosorbide dinitrate.
Monitor weight, renal function, and electrolytes. Provide advice about smoking, alcohol, and monitoring symptoms. Give regular influenza and pneumococcal vaccinations.

footnotes.footnote: Abbreviations: ACE angiotensin-converting enzyme; ARB, angiotensin receptor blocker; BNP, B-type natriuretic peptide; LFT, liver function tests; TFT, thyroid function tests.
